title: Why things always shift on their own until they stop changing
phenomenon: A cup of hot water left alone cools toward the room, fast at first, then slower. A radioactive sample does the same thing with the number of nuclei. Nobody has to touch it.
invariant: The fraction by which it deviates from equilibrium shrinks over time with the same time constant. Half-life = τ·ln2, independent of how large the deviation is.
force_invariant: The amount still away from equilibrium changes in proportion to itself, so the drop is fast at first and then slower. The time to cut that deviation in half does not depend on how large the starting deviation is. A drop of a fixed number of degrees takes longer when you are closer to the room than when you are far from it.
operator: dx/dt = -(x - x_eq)/tau    (first order; the half-life is tau ln 2)
check_yourself: The time to halve the temperature difference from the room does not depend on the starting difference. Why, then, does a drop of ten degrees take longer when the water is already close to the room? Because ten degrees is a larger fraction of a small remaining difference than of a large one.
entry_question: Why does hot water cool down on its own? I never touched it.
transfer: Radioactive decay, half-life independent of the starting number
A capacitor discharging through a resistor
boundary: When the temperature difference is large, radiation goes as the fourth power of the temperature and one time constant is not enough. If the object has no single temperature, the one-variable picture fails first.
reality_meaning: The same exponential shows up wherever a difference shrinks in proportion to itself: a radioactive sample, a draining capacitor, a temperature difference.
game_instance: A radioactive sample, or a capacitor draining through a resistor.

support.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, Chapter 24 (Transients), and radioactive decay
support.note: The half-life is a time to halve the deviation. It does not depend on the starting size.

title: Money does not appear out of nowhere, so where does it go
phenomenon: A tub filling at one end and draining at the other can rise, hold, or fall. The level cares about the difference, not about either flow by itself.
invariant: With no sources or sinks, the total is strictly conserved: d(∫ρ)/dt = 0. To say there is less, you must point to where it went.
force_invariant: In the energy lectures the rule is bookkeeping. If the amount changes, the difference between what came in and what went out has to account for it. With no source and no sink the total does not change, and a claim that it did has to say where it went.
operator: partial rho / partial t + divergence of J = S
check_yourself: A team's headcount did not change, yet someone says there are fewer people. What has to be added before that sentence can be checked? Where they went. Otherwise it is not a conservation statement.
entry_question: Why does the water level rise? I have been draining it the whole time.
transfer: Heat leaving one body and entering another
boundary: The region has to be named first. Leave out the source term and an open system is miscounted. A quantity can look conserved only because the window was too short to see the leak.
reality_meaning: When someone says it increased or it decreased, ask where it came from and where it went.
game_instance: Charge in a region: the change equals what flowed in minus what flowed out.

support.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, Chapter 4, Conservation of Energy
support.note: A change in the books has to equal what came in minus what went out.

title: Why some things start out unremarkable and later cannot be stopped
phenomenon: A snowball picks up more as it gets bigger. That is the same shape as a chain reaction: each step multiplies what is already there, for as long as the factor stays above one.
invariant: Doubling time is constant: t₂ = ln2/k. No matter how big it is now, doubling takes the same time.
force_invariant: The growth is in proportion to what is already there, not a fixed amount added each step. While that factor stays above one, the doubling time is constant. It holds only until something runs out; then the curve bends over.
operator: dx/dt = +k x  =>  x(t) = x0 exp(k t), with k > 0
check_yourself: A chain goes from 100 to about 1000 in seven days, multiplying rather than adding a fixed number. The doubling time stays about two days. Adding a fixed daily amount instead predicts far too little by day fourteen.
entry_question: Why does a snowball get bigger the more it rolls? Anyone who rolled one as a kid knows it does, but why?
transfer: A nuclear chain reaction with reproduction factor greater than one
Any proportional growth before a supply runs out
boundary: It holds only while the supply is not the limit. At a ceiling the curve bends into an S.
reality_meaning: To see whether a chain will run, you need the multiplication factor, the doubling time, and where the supply runs out.
game_instance: Neutrons in a supercritical assembly, each generation larger by the same factor.

support.source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, the chain-reaction chapters; The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, exponential growth
support.note: The snowball is the same shape as a chain reaction. The lecture form is the chain reaction, not a claim that he lectured on snow.

title: Why walking with a full cup of water is steadier
phenomenon: Walking with a full cup is the same problem as a damped oscillator. Correct too slowly and the tilt gets away. Correct too hard, late, and you overshoot and it sloshes.
invariant: Disturbances are suppressed. Three regimes are separated by the damping ratio ζ: overdamped (slow but no overshoot), critically damped (fastest without overshoot), underdamped (fast but sways back and forth).
force_invariant: Volume I, Chapter 24 separates three regimes. Light damping: it swings and the swings shrink. Heavy damping: it creeps back and does not swing. Critical damping: it returns as fast as it can without swinging past rest. The cup spills when the correction and the delay are not in the regime you wanted.
operator: x double-dot + 2 zeta omega x-dot + omega^2 x = 0
check_yourself: Why does a correction that is strong, but late, turn into sloshing? The push arrives for a state that has already passed, so the motion rings. That is the underdamped side of Chapter 24.
entry_question: Walking with a full cup of water, the more careful I am the more I spill, while quick small steps do not spill. Why?
transfer: Volume I, Chapter 24, the three damping regimes
A circuit with resistance, inductance, and capacitance
boundary: Too much gain, or too much delay, turns damping into oscillation. Far into a nonlinear regime, one damping ratio is no longer the whole story.
reality_meaning: Holding a drifting thing still is a match of gain and delay. Both a late correction and an oversized one spill the cup.
game_instance: A mass on a spring, returned to rest with too little friction or too much.

support.source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, Chapter 24, Transients
support.note: The cup is the same three regimes as the damped oscillator in that chapter.
